1. Grammar: Verb tenses review
1.1. Present simple – present continuous
The Present Simple is used for general or habitual actions, while the Present
Continuous is used for actions happening at the moment or temporary
actions.
The Present Simple can also express universal truths, whereas the Present
Continuous cannot.
The Present Simple has third-person singular forms with "s" (e.g., he/she/it
works), while the Present Continuous uses the base form of the verb with
"ing" (e.g., he/she/it is working).
Present Simple. Structure:
• Subject + base form of the verb
Examples:
• I eat breakfast every morning
• They live in New York
• In the third person singular: Subject + base form of the verb + "s"
Examples:
• She works in an office
• He goes to the gym
• Negative form: Subject + don’t/doesn’t (in the 3rd person) + base
form of the verb
Examples:
|FP Euroformac Página 5 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
• I don’t eat breakfast every morning
• She doesn’t work in an office
• Interrogative form: Do/Does + Subject + base form of the verb +?
Examples:
• Do you live in New York?
• Does he go to the gym?
Present Continuous. Structure:
• Subject + present form of "to be" + verb -ing
Examples:
• I am eating lunch right now
• They are studying for their exams
• Negative form: Subject + negative form of “to be” + verb -ing
Examples:
• I am not eating lunch right now
• They are not studying for their exams
• Interrogative form: present form of "to be" + Subject + verb –ing +?
Examples:
• Are you eating lunch right now?
• Are they studying for their exams?
|FP Euroformac Página 6 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
1.2. Past simple – past continuous
The Past Simple is used for completed actions at a specific point in the past,
while the Past Continuous is used for actions in progress in the past.
The Past Simple is often used to narrate events in a chronological sequence,
while the Past Continuous emphasizes the duration or exact moment of an
action in the past.
Past Simple. Structure:
• For regular verbs: Subject + past form of the verb ("-ed")
Examples:
• I visited Paris last summer
• She watched a movie yesterday
• For irregular verbs: Subject + past form of the verb (no fixed rule)
Examples:
• He went to the store
• They ate pizza for dinner
• Negative form: Subject + did not / didn’t + base form of the verb
Examples:
• I didn’t visit Paris last summer
• He didn’t go to the store
• Interrogative form: Did + Subject + base form of the verb +?
Examples:
|FP Euroformac Página 7 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
• Did you visit Paris last summer?
• Did he go to the store?
Past Continuous. Structure:
• Subject + was/were + verb -ing
Examples:
• I was reading a book when the phone rang
• They were playing soccer at 3 o'clock yesterday
• Negative form: Subject + wasn’t/weren’t + verb -ing
Examples:
• I wasn’t reading a book when the phone rang
• They weren’t playing soccer at 3 o'clock yesterday
• Interrogative form: Was/Were + Subject + verb –ing +?
Examples:
• Were you reading a book when the phone rang?
• Was she playing soccer at 3 o'clock yesterday?
1.3. Present perfect simple – present perfect
continuous
The Present Perfect Simple is often used to describe actions or events that
have relevance to the present, completed actions in the past, and
experiences, while the Present Perfect Continuous is used to emphasize the
duration of an action that started in the past and is continuing into the
present.
|FP Euroformac Página 8 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
The Present Perfect Simple focuses on the
result or completion of an action, while the
Present Perfect Continuous emphasizes
the duration and often implies an ongoing
action.
Present Perfect Simple. Structure:
• Subject + have/has + past participle of the verb
Examples:
• I have visited Paris several times. (Relevance to the present)
• She has finished her homework. (Completion of an action in the
past)
• Negative form: Subject + haven’t/hasn’t + past participle of the verb
Examples:
• I haven’t visited Paris
• She hasn’t finished her homework
<Important>
We use “never” in negative sentences to emphasize that a
certain action or experience has not happened at any time in
a person's life up to the present. In this case the verb must be
affirmative since “never” turns the whole sentence into
negative.
Example: I have never eaten sushi. (Indicates that the person has not had
the experience of eating sushi at any point in their life.)
|FP Euroformac Página 9 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
• Interrogative form: Have/Has + Subject + past participle of the verb +?
Examples:
• Has she finished her homework?
• Have you had lunch today?
<Important>
We frequently use "ever" in questions to inquire if a particular
action or experience has occurred at any point in a person's
life up to the present moment.
Example: Have you ever traveled to Europe? (Asking if the person has had
the experience of traveling to Europe at any time in their life.)
Present Perfect Continuous. Structure:
• Subject + have/has + been + verb -ing
Examples:
• I have been reading for two hours. (Emphasizing the duration)
• She has been studying all morning. (Ongoing action into the
present)
• Negative form: Subject + haven’t/hasn’t + been + verb -ing
Examples:
• I haven’t been reading for two hours.
• She hasn’t been studying all morning.
• Interrogative form: Have/Has + Subject + been + verb -ing +?

• Have you been reading for two hours?

2. Effective and formal communication
Effective and formal communication is an important skill in professional
contexts. It enables us to convey ideas, build relationships, and achieve our
goals with precision and professionalism. Here we will explore the essentials
of effective and formal communication, providing valuable insights and
practical tips to enhance our communication skills for success in various
settings.
2.1. Greetings, receptions and farewells
Effective communication often begins with the exchange of greetings,
setting the tone for a conversation, and concludes with a suitable farewell.
The choice of greeting, reception, and farewell can vary depending on the
formality of the situation, and understanding these social conventions is
crucial for establishing a positive interaction. Here are some examples:
|FP Euroformac Página 12 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
Greetings:
• "Hello" and "Hi": These are universal and versatile greetings suitable
for both formal and informal settings.
• "Good morning," "Good afternoon," and "Good evening": These
greetings are more time-specific.
• "How are you?": This common greeting inquires about someone's
well-being and is a polite way to show interest in the other person's
state of mind.
Receptions:
• "Nice to meet you": This reception is often used when meeting
someone for the first time and conveys a friendly and welcoming
attitude.
• "It's a pleasure to see you again": This is a warm reception for someone
you've met before, and it expresses your delight in reuniting.
• "Welcome to our team" or "Welcome to the event/meeting": These
receptions are suitable for welcoming
someone into a group, workplace, or
specific occasion. They are particularly
common in professional or organizational
settings.
Farewells:
• "Goodbye" and "Farewell": These are standard farewells used in both
formal and informal situations.
|FP Euroformac Página 13 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
• "Nice talking to you": A friendly and informal farewell that expresses
appreciation for the conversation.
• "See you later": These farewells
suggest the hope of future
encounters and are suitable for
both casual and closer
relationships.
2.2. Politeness and formality in communication
Effective communication is not just about the words we use; it's also about
the tone and expressions we use to convey respect and consideration.
Politeness and formality play a crucial role in our everyday and professional
interactions. Here are some examples:
Politeness:
• "Please" is commonly used to make requests.
• "Thank you" is commonly used to express gratitude.
• "You're welcome" is the response to "Thank you" and shows
acknowledgment of gratitude.
• "Excuse me" is used to get someone's attention.
• "Pardon me" is a way to politely ask someone to repeat.
• "I'm sorry" is used to apologize or express regret.
• "May I?" is a polite way to seek permission.
Formality:
|FP Euroformac Página 14 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
• In formal situations, titles and honorifics are used, such as "Mr.," "Mrs.,"
"Miss," "Sir," or "Madam."
• Addressing someone by their last name with a title, like "Mr. Smith" or
"Dr. Johnson," is common in formal settings.
• "Sir" and "Madam" can be used in a polite and respectful manner,
especially when you don't know the person's name.
2.3. Seeking clarification, reception and confirmation
In effective communication, seeking clarification, repetition, and
confirmation are essential techniques to ensure that information is clearly
understood and that misunderstandings are minimized. Whether you're in a
professional setting, discussing a complex topic, or learning something
new, these strategies can help foster better comprehension and facilitate
smooth conversations. Here are some examples:
Clarification:
• Could you please explain that in more detail?
• I'm not quite following. Can you break it down step by step?
• Could you elaborate on the technical aspects of the issue?
• I need more information to fully grasp the situation.
Repetition:
• I'm sorry, could you repeat the last part of your explanation?
• I'm sorry, I missed that. Can you please go over it one more time?
• Could you kindly repeat the key points you just mentioned?
|FP Euroformac Página 15 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
• I got lost during your explanation. Could you run through it again?
Confirmation:
• Just to make sure I understood correctly, you mean...
• If I understand correctly, you're saying that...
• Just to confirm, you're suggesting that we implement this solution,
right?
• So, to be clear, you're recommending that we proceed with this
update?
2.4. Indentifying main and secondary ideas in
presentations and debates
Understanding the main and secondary ideas in presentations and debates
is essential for effective communication and decision-making.
Main Ideas are the central points or key takeaways from a presentation or
debate. They often serve as the core message or thesis.
Secondary Ideas are supporting points or details that provide evidence or
context for the main ideas.
Example:
Imagine you're attending a presentation on a new network security protocol:
Main Idea: "The new security protocol significantly enhances our network's
safety."
|FP Euroformac Página 16 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
Secondary Ideas: "It uses advanced encryption algorithms, offers real-time
threat detection, and simplifies user authentication."
2.5. Expressing opinions, preferences, tastes, and
complaints in a profesional context
In a professional context, effectively expressing
opinions, preferences, tastes, and complaints is
essential for clear communication and problem-
solving. Here are some examples for each of these aspects:
Opinions:
An opinion is a personal belief or judgment about a particular topic. In a
professional setting, it's important to express your opinions respectfully and
provide reasoning or evidence to support your viewpoint.
Example 1: "In my opinion, implementing a remote work policy would
enhance work-life balance and increase employee satisfaction. This is
based on the fact that many studies have shown improved productivity
when employees have the flexibility to work from home."
Example 2: "I believe that expanding our product line to include eco-
friendly options aligns with the growing consumer demand for sustainable
products. It could be a strategic move to capture a new market segment."
Preferences:
|FP Euroformac Página 17 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
Preferences refer to what you like or favor. When expressing preferences
professionally, it's important to provide context and explain how they align
with your work or goals.
Example 1: "I have a preference for using Google Workspace for email and
collaboration tools because it integrates well with our existing systems,
streamlining our workflow."
Example 2: "I prefer a structured agenda for meetings as it helps keep
discussions focused and ensures that we cover all important topics
efficiently."
Tastes:
Tastes relate to your personal likes or dislikes. When discussing tastes in a
professional context, it's important to tie them to relevant decisions or
processes.
Example 1: "My taste in design leans towards a clean and modern aesthetic,
which I believe resonates well with our target audience and aligns with our
brand image."
Example 2: "I personally enjoy a collaborative work environment where
ideas are openly shared. I find it encourages innovation and team
cohesion."
Complaints:
|FP Euroformac Página 18 de 27
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 1
Complaints are expressions of dissatisfaction or concerns. In a professional
context, it's crucial to raise complaints constructively and propose solutions
when possible.
Example 1: "I've received complaints from several clients about the delayed
response time from our customer support team. I suggest we implement a
ticketing system to improve efficiency."
Example 2: "I want to address a recurring issue in our project management
where tasks are not clearly defined. This has led to confusion and delays.
Let's consider using a project management tool to assign and track tasks
more effectively."
Remember that in a professional context, it's important to maintain a
respectful and open-minded tone. Constructive communication is key to
resolving issues, making informed decisions, and fostering a positive work
environment. Always provide rationale, data, or examples to support your
opinions and preferences, and offer solutions when expressing complaints.

1. Grammar: Personal pronouns
Personal pronouns replace nouns and stand for the people or things
involved. They are categorized based on their role in a sentence.
As we already know, the SUBJECT PRONOUNS are:
SUBJECT PRONOUMS
I
You
He/she/it
We
They
OBJECT PRONOUNS
Object pronouns are used in sentences as the receivers of the action
performed by the subject. They replace or stand in for the person or thing
that is the direct or indirect object of the verb.
|FP Euroformac Página 5 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
OBJECT PRONOUMS
Me
You
Him/her/it
Us
Them
Examples:
• My mom loves me.
• They want to join us for dinner.
POSSESSIVE PRONOUNS
Possessive adjectives
These work like adjectives. They point to a specific noun.
|FP Euroformac Página 6 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
POSSESIVE ADJECTIVES
My
Your
His/her/its
Our
Their
Possessive Pronouns
These stand alone. They don't need a specific noun to make sense.
POSSESIVE PRONOUMS
Mine
Yours
His/hers/its
Ours
|FP Euroformac Página 7 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
Theirs
Example:
• My car is blue. Yours is red. (The possessive adjective “my” needs a
noun, “car”. Once the noun is said and known, the possessive pronoun
“yours” involves the noun itself because we already know it from the
context).
REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS
These pronouns are used when the subject and the object of the action are
the same person or thing.
REFLEXIVE PRONOUMS
Myself
Yourself
Himself / Herself / Itself
Ourselves
Yourselves
|FP Euroformac Página 8 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
Examples:
• I hurt myself while cooking.
• Have you ever asked yourself why?
RELATIVE PRONOUNS
Relative pronouns are words that introduce relative clauses in a sentence. A
relative clause provides additional information about a noun or pronoun in
the main clause. Relative pronouns not only introduce these clauses but also
serve as the subject or object within the relative clause.
Common relative pronouns in English include:
Who: Used for people.
Example: The person who called you is waiting outside.
Whom: Also used for people, particularly as the object of a verb or
preposition.
Example: The student, whom I admire, won the award.
Which: Used for animals and things.
Example: The book, which is on the table, is mine.
|FP Euroformac Página 9 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
That: Used for people, animals, and things. It is more flexible and can often
be used in place of "who" or "which."
Example: The car that is parked outside is mine.
Whose: Indicates possession and is used for people, animals, and things.
Example: The woman whose bag was lost has found it.
1.1. First and second conditional
FIRST CONDITIONAL
The first conditional is used to talk about real or very likely future situations. It
consists of two clauses: the "if" clause (conditional clause) and the main
clause.
Structure:
If + present simple, will + base form of the verb.
Examples:
• If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
• If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
• If she calls me, I will answer.
|FP Euroformac Página 10 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
SECOND CONDITIONAL
The second conditional is used to talk about hypothetical or unreal situations
in the present or future. It also has an "if" clause and a main clause.
Structure:
If + past simple, would + base form of the verb.
Examples:
• If I won the lottery, I would travel around the world.
• If he studied more, he would get better grades.
• If they invited us to the party, we would bring a gift.
|FP Euroformac Página 11 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
2. Professional effectiveness
2.1. Communication dynamics
Common Formulas for Initiating, Sustaining, and Concluding
Conversations in Various Settings.
Effective communication is a cornerstone of successful interactions in
diverse environments, ranging from telephone calls to job interviews.
Understanding and employing common formulas for initiating, maintaining,
and concluding conversations is crucial for fostering meaningful
connections and achieving desired outcomes.
Initiating Conversations:
1. Polite Greetings:
Example: "Hello, this is [Your Name]. How are you today?"
This formula establishes a positive tone and creates a welcoming
atmosphere at the beginning of a conversation.
2. Introduction of Purpose:
Example: "I'm calling to discuss [topic] and explore potential
solutions."
Clearly stating the purpose sets expectations and provides a guide
for the conversation.
|FP Euroformac Página 12 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
Maintaining Conversations:
1. Active Listening and Acknowledgment:
Example: "I understand your perspective. Could you elaborate on
[specific point]?"
Actively listening and acknowledging the other person's input fosters
engagement and demonstrates respect.
2. Open-Ended Questions:
Example: "How do you address [issue] in your department?"
Encouraging open-ended questions stimulates thoughtful responses
and promotes in-depth discussions.
Concluding Conversations:
1. Summarization and Confirmation:
Example: "To recap, we've discussed [key points]. Does that
accurately capture our conversation?"
Summarizing ensures mutual understanding and allows for any
necessary clarifications before concluding.
2. Expressing Gratitude and Next Steps:
Example: "Thank you for your time. I will follow up with [action] by
[date]."
Expressing gratitude and outlining the next steps establishes

2.2. Handling complaints
Handling complaints is a crucial skill in both personal and professional
settings. It involves not only addressing the immediate issue but also
managing emotions, fostering understanding, and building positive
relationships. This theory explores the key elements of effective complaint
handling, emphasizing language use and strategies.
1. Empathy as the Foundation:
Effective complaint handling starts with empathy. Begin by
acknowledging the customer's feelings and concerns. Examples:
• "I understand how frustrating this must be for you."
• "I'm sorry to hear about your experience."
2. Active Listening:
Encourage open communication by actively listening to the
complaint. Show engagement through expressions. Examples:
• "I appreciate you bringing this to our attention."
• "Could you please share more details about the issue?"
3. Clarification and Confirmation:
Ensure a clear understanding of the complaint by paraphrasing and
seeking confirmation. Examples:
• "If I understand correctly, you are saying..."
• "Just to clarify, are you referring to...?"
4. Solution-Oriented Language:
Shift the focus towards finding solutions. Use positive and solution-
oriented language. Examples:
|FP Euroformac Página 15 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 2
• "Let's work together to resolve this issue."
• "I'm committed to finding a solution that works for you."
5. Offering Alternatives:
Provide alternatives or options to resolve the complaint. Examples:
• "We could try [solution A] or [solution B]. What do you think?"
• "I suggest [alternative] as another possible resolution. How
does that sound?"
6. Apologizing and Taking Responsibility:
When appropriate, take responsibility for any mistakes and offer a
sincere apology. Examples:
• "I apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused."
• "We take responsibility for the oversight and are committed to
making it right."
7. Follow-Up Assurance:
Assure the complainant that their concerns are taken seriously and
that follow-up actions will be taken. Examples:
• "I will personally ensure that this matter is investigated
thoroughly."
• "We will follow up with you within [specified time] to update you
on the progress."
8. Language of Appreciation:
End the interaction on a positive note by expressing appreciation for
their feedback. Examples:
• "Thank you for bringing this to our attention. Your feedback
helps us improve."

make things right."

1. Grammar: Modal verbs
Modal verbs are a category of auxiliary verbs used to express modality, which
is the speaker's attitude or the likelihood of the action in the main verb. They
add nuance to the meaning of the main verb in a sentence. Here are the main
modal verbs:
CAN
Used to express ability, possibility, permission, or a request.
Examples:
• Ability: She can speak three languages.
• Possibility: It can rain later.
• Permission: Can I borrow your pen?
• Request: Can you help me with this?
• Its negative form is can’t.
COULD
Similar to 'can,' but often used in more polite or formal situations. Also used
for past ability.
Examples:
• Polite request: Could you please pass the salt?
• Past ability: When I was younger, I could run very fast.
• Its negative form is couldn’t.
|FP Euroformac Página 6 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
MAY
Used to express possibility, probability, or permission, often in a more formal
context.
Examples:
• Possibility: It may rain tomorrow.
• Permission: May I come in?
• Its negative form is may not.
MIGHT
Similar to 'may' but generally implies a lower probability or a more uncertain
situation.
Example:
• He might be at the party, but I'm not sure.
• Its negative form is might not.
MUST
Expresses necessity, obligation, or a strong
assumption.
Examples:
• Necessity: You must finish your homework
before going out.
• Assumption: The door is open, so he must be inside.
• Its negative form is mustn’t.
|FP Euroformac Página 7 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
SHOULD
Indicates advice, suggestion, or obligation.
Examples:
• Advice: You should see a doctor if the pain persists.
• Obligation: Students should attend all classes.
• Its negative form is shouldn’t.

2.1. Organization of the information in technical texts
Technical texts are designed to convey complex information in a clear and
structured manner. Various elements such as indices, titles, headings,
tables, outlines, and graphics play crucial roles in organizing information
effectively. The organization of information in technical texts serves to
enhance readability, comprehension, and accessibility. Here's a breakdown
of these elements and how they contribute to the overall organization:
• Indices:
Indices, also known as indexes, provide a comprehensive list of topics
or keywords along with the corresponding page numbers where
readers can find information related to those topics.
Example: In a technical manual, an index might include entries such as
"Troubleshooting," "Installation," and "Maintenance," guiding readers
to relevant sections throughout the document.
• Titles and Headings:
Titles and headings serve as signposts, dividing the text into
meaningful sections. They provide a hierarchical structure, indicating
the importance and relationships between different parts of the
content.
Example: In a software development document, a title might be
"System Architecture," and under it, there could be headings like
"Database Design," "User Interface," and "Security Measures."
|FP Euroformac Página 9 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
• Tables:
Tables are used to present organized sets of data in a visually
accessible format. They help in comparing information, identifying
patterns, and conveying complex relationships more efficiently than
plain text.
Example: In a scientific research paper, a table might display
experimental results with columns for variables such as "Time,"
"Temperature," and "Observations," facilitating a clear understanding
of the data.
• Outlines:
Outlines provide a structural overview of the document, presenting a
hierarchical arrangement of main topics and subtopics. They offer
readers a roadmap for navigating the content.
Example: In a business proposal, the outline could start with sections
like "Executive Summary," followed by "Market Analysis," "Product
Description," and "Financial Projections," outlining the key
components of the proposal.
• Graphics:
Graphics, including charts, graphs, diagrams, and illustrations, are
used to visually represent complex information. They can enhance
understanding, provide clarity, and offer a quick overview of key
concepts.
Example: In a technical manual for assembling a piece of furniture, a
diagram could visually guide users through the step-by-step
assembly process, complementing the written instructions.
|FP Euroformac Página 10 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
2.2. Types of professional documents
In the professional sector, various types of documents are utilized to
communicate information, guidelines, and standards. Each type serves a
specific purpose and caters to the needs of different stakeholders.
Here's an overview of some common types of professional sector
documents:
• Manuals:
Manuals are comprehensive documents that provide detailed
information and instructions about a product, process, system, or
equipment. They guide users on how to operate, maintain,
troubleshoot, or assemble something.
Example: An employee handbook in a company can serve as a manual,
outlining policies, procedures, and guidelines for employees.
• Instructions:
Instructions are documents that guide users through a specific task or
process. They are often concise, step-by-step, and focus on
providing clear guidance for performing a particular activity.
Example: User manuals for electronic devices often include
instructions on how to set up the device, use its features, and
troubleshoot common issues.
• Reports:
Reports are documents that convey information, findings, or insights
derived from research, analysis, or investigations. They are often used
to inform decision-making within an organization or to communicate
externally.
|FP Euroformac Página 11 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
Example: A business performance report might include data on sales,
market trends, and financial metrics, providing insights for
management and stakeholders.
• Safety Standards:
Safety standards documents outline rules, regulations, and
guidelines aimed at ensuring the safety of individuals, equipment, or
environments. These documents are crucial in industries where safety
is a primary concern.
Example: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
standards in the United States provide guidelines for workplace
safety, including regulations on equipment usage and hazard
communication.
• Protocols:
Protocols are documents that specify a set of rules or procedures to
be followed in a particular situation. They are common in scientific and
medical fields, outlining standardized procedures for experiments or
treatments.
Example: A laboratory protocol might detail the steps to follow when
conducting a specific experiment, including materials, methods, and
safety precautions.
• Policies and Procedures:
Documents outlining organizational policies and procedures provide
guidelines for employees on how to conduct themselves, handle
various situations, and adhere to company standards.
An HR manual may include policies on employee conduct, leave
policies, and procedures for addressing workplace issues.
|FP Euroformac Página 12 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
• Contracts:
Contracts are legal documents that outline the terms and conditions
of agreements between parties. They specify the rights and
obligations of each party involved.
Example: A service contract between a client and a service provider
might include details on services to be provided, payment terms, and
dispute resolution mechanisms.
2.3. Localization and selection of information
Localization and selection of relevant information refer to the efficient
process of reading to identify the main theme and extract specific
information from a text. This approach involves two key components: quick
reading and focused reading.
1. Quick Reading
Quick reading, also known as skimming or scanning, is a rapid
overview of the text to grasp the main idea. During quick reading,
individuals glance over headings, subheadings, and the first and last
sentences of paragraphs. This technique helps to get a sense of the
overall structure and theme of the text without delving into every
detail.
Example: Imagine you are given an article
on the impact of climate change on
biodiversity. During quick reading, you
might skim through the headings, look at
the introductory and concluding
|FP Euroformac Página 13 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
paragraphs, and check for any bolded or highlighted keywords
related to climate change and biodiversity.
2. Focused Reading
Focused reading involves a more in-depth examination of the text to
locate specific information or details. Once the main theme is
identified through quick reading, focused reading allows the reader to
concentrate on particular sections or paragraphs relevant to their
information needs. This method helps in extracting details and gaining
a deeper understanding of specific topics.
Example: Continuing with the climate change and biodiversity article,
after a quick reading, you may decide to focus on a section that
discusses the effects on a particular
ecosystem. Focused reading in this context
involves carefully going through that
section, looking for specific examples,
statistics, or case studies related to the
impact on biodiversity.
The localization and selection of relevant
information align with the cognitive
processes of information retrieval and
comprehension. By quickly identifying the main theme, readers
create a mental framework for understanding the context. Focused
reading, then, allows for a targeted exploration of the text to extract
details, supporting a more thorough understanding of specific
aspects.
Benefits:
|FP Euroformac Página 14 de 24
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 3
• Time Efficiency: Localization and selection of relevant
information streamline the reading process, saving time by
avoiding unnecessary scrutiny of irrelevant details.
• Improved Retention: By first grasping the main theme and then
focusing on specific information, readers are more likely to
retain key details and concepts.
• Enhanced Comprehension: The combination of quick and
focused reading promotes a balanced approach to
information processing, facilitating a comprehensive
understanding of the material.

Literal comprehension involves grasping the surface-level meaning of
a text. We need to understand the who, what, when, where, and why of
the information presented.
Inferential Comprehension:
Inferential comprehension goes beyond the explicit information and
requires readers to draw conclusions based on implied or suggested
details in the text.
Evaluative Comprehension:
Evaluative comprehension involves forming opinions and judgments
about the text and considering its validity, reliability, and relevance.

Understanding the structure of a text is crucial. This includes

identifying the main ideas and supporting details.
Identifying Tone and Style:
Recognizing the author's tone and style provides insight into the
intended message. It includes identifying formal or informal language,

Exploring Language Devices:
Language devices such as metaphors, similes, and symbolism can
convey deeper meanings. Understanding these devices enhances
comprehension and appreciation of the text.

sections of a text to create a unified understanding. It requires critical

1. Grammar: Future tenses
• WILL
Structure:
Subject + will + base form of the verb
Negative: subject + will not / won’t + base form of the verb
Usage:
Predictions: Used for expressing future events that are not planned
but are based on the speaker's opinion, belief, or intuition.
Example:
In five years the president of the US will be a woman.
Promises: Employed to make commitments or assurances about
future actions.
Example:
I will help you with your homework.
Offers: Used to express willingness to do something for someone in
the future.
Example:
Will you come to the party?
|FP Euroformac Página 5 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• BE GOING TO
Structure:
Subject + am/is/are + going to + base form of the verb
Negative: subject + negative form of the verb to be + base form of the
verb
Usage:
Intentions/Plans: Used to indicate future intentions or plans, often
based on current evidence or circumstances.
Example:
I am going to study Law.
Predictions: Similar to "will," it is used when there is clear evidence or
intention in the present.
Example:
It's going to be a great movie.
• PRESENT SIMPLE (as future)
Usage:
Scheduled Events: Applied to describe events that are part of a
timetable or schedule in the future.
Example:
The train leaves at 9 am tomorrow.
|FP Euroformac Página 6 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• PRESENT CONTINUOUS (as future)
Usage:
Arrangements/Plans: Used to describe future arrangements or plans,
often with a sense of immediacy.
Example:
We are meeting for lunch at 12 PM.
Scheduled Events: Similar to the present simple, but with an emphasis
on the arrangement aspect.
Example:
She is flying to London next week.
• BE GOING TO vs. PRESENT CONTINUOUS
While “Be Going To” expresses intentions or plans for future actions
based on present circumstances or intentions, “Present Continuous”
expresses arrangements or plans already scheduled in the future.
Examples of “be going to”
• I am going to start a new project next week. (It could be
cancelled at the last moment)
• Look at those dark clouds. It's going to rain. (But we can never
be sure about the weather)
Examples of “future continuous”
|FP Euroformac Página 7 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• We are meeting for dinner at 7 PM. (We have a reservation)
• She is flying to Paris next month. (She already has the plane
tickets)
<Important>
Keep in mind that in many cases, some of these tense (as be
going to and present continuous) are interchangeable
without significantly changing the meaning of the sentence.

2.1. Documents for job placement
The objective of this lesson is to understand the key elements and best
practices for drafting essential documents related to the job placement
process, including the Curriculum Vitae (CV), Cover Letter, and Job
Application Response.
• CURRICULUM VITAE (CV)
A CV is a comprehensive document highlighting an individual's
education, work experience, skills, and achievements.
Structure:
• Contact Information: Name, phone number, email, and
LinkedIn profile (if applicable).
|FP Euroformac Página 9 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• Objective or Summary: A brief statement outlining career
goals or a summary of qualifications.
• Education: List academic qualifications in reverse
chronological order.
• Work Experience: Detail professional experience, emphasizing
achievements and responsibilities.
• Skills: Showcase relevant skills, both technical and soft.
• Achievements and Awards: Highlight any notable
accomplishments or recognition.
• References: Optionally, include references or state available
upon request.
Examples:
Objective/Summary:
"Dedicated marketing professional with over 5 years of experience in
strategic planning and campaign management, seeking a challenging
role to leverage creativity and drive results."
Work Experience:
“Marketing Manager, XYZ Company (2018-2022)”:
Managed a team of 5, increasing client retention by 20% through
targeted marketing campaigns.
Skills:
• Digital Marketing: SEO, SEM, Social Media Management
• Analytical: Data Analysis, Market Research
|FP Euroformac Página 10 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• COVER LETTER
A cover letter introduces the candidate to the employer, emphasizing
why they are suitable for the position.
Structure:
• Contact Information: Similar to CV, include name, phone,
email, and date.
• Salutation: Address the hiring manager by name if possible; if
not, use a general salutation.
• Introduction: Clearly state the position you are applying for and
how you learned about it.
• Body: Highlight relevant skills, experiences, and achievements.
Explain how they align with the job requirements.
• Closing: Express gratitude for consideration, include a call to
action, and sign off professionally.
Examples:
Introduction:
"I am writing to express my interest in the Marketing Manager position
advertised on your company's website."
Body:
"With a proven track record in developing and executing successful
marketing strategies, I believe my skills in digital marketing and team
leadership make me an ideal candidate for this role."
Closing:
|FP Euroformac Página 11 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
"Thank you for considering my application. I am excited about the
opportunity to contribute to [Company Name]. I look forward to the
possibility of discussing how my skills align with your needs in more
detail."
• JOB APPLICATION RESPONSE
A response to a job offer, demonstrating continued interest and
providing any additional requested information.
Structure:
• Express Gratitude: Begin by thanking the employer for the
offer.
• Confirmation: Confirm acceptance of the offer and express
enthusiasm.
• Details: Provide any necessary details, such as start date or
requested documentation.
• Closing: Reiterate appreciation and express excitement about
joining the team.
Examples:
Express Gratitude:
"Thank you for offering me the position of Marketing Coordinator at
[Company Name]."
Confirmation:
"I am thrilled about the opportunity and am eager to contribute my
skills to the success of the marketing team."
|FP Euroformac Página 12 de 22

Details:
"I am available to start on [specified date] and will ensure all required
documentation is submitted promptly."
Closing:
"Once again, thank you for this opportunity. I am looking forward to
being a part of [Company Name] and contributing to its continued
success."
In conclusion, understanding how to craft effective documents for
the job placement process is crucial
for career advancement. Remember
to tailor each document to the specific
job requirements and company
culture. Regularly update your CV and
cover letter to reflect your evolving skills and experiences.
2.2. Telematic communication
In the professional world, effective communication via email is crucial. It
reflects your professionalism and can significantly impact how you are
perceived by colleagues, clients, or potential employers. Here we will
master the art of composing courteous and formal professional emails by
understanding the key formulas and etiquette.
Courtesy Formulas in Professional Emails
|FP Euroformac Página 13 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• Salutation:
Always start with a polite salutation, addressing the recipient
appropriately.
Examples:
"Dear Mr/Mrs/Ms. Smith," or "Dear [Recipient's Name],"
• Expressing Gratitude:
When applicable, express gratitude for the recipient's time,
assistance, or consideration.
Examples:
"Thank you for your prompt response."
"Thank you for considering my proposal."
• Polite Requests:
Make requests politely, using courteous language.
Examples:
"Could you please provide more details about..."
"I would appreciate it if you could share your insights on this matter."
• Closing:
End the email with a polite closing phrase.
Examples:
"Best regards," or "Sincerely,"
|FP Euroformac Página 14 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
Formality Formulas in Professional Emails
• Formal Language:
Use formal language appropriate for a professional setting.
Examples:
"I am writing to inquire about..."
"I am reaching out to discuss the upcoming project."
• Avoiding Informal Expressions:
Avoid using overly casual language or emojis in professional
correspondence.
Avoid phrases like "Hey" or informal abbreviations.
• Clear and Concise Language:
Be clear and concise in your communication, avoiding unnecessary
details.
Example:
"I wanted to follow up on our discussion regarding..."
Fax:
Fax machines send documents over telephone lines. To send one, place the
document in the machine, dial the recipient's number, and press send. The
document is scanned, sent as signals, and printed at the other end.

Telex:
Telex lets businesses send text messages electronically. Messages are:
• typed on machine
• transmitted over phone lines
• printed out at the receiving end.
It's reliable but old-fashioned, replaced
by email today.
Telegram:
Telegrams are like old-fashioned text
messages. Messages are sent in
Morse code over telegraph wires,
then decoded and delivered. They
were fast in the past but are rarely
used now, replaced by emails and
texts.
2.3. Professional terminology related to job
placement
Here are some terminology:
• Job Posting: A public announcement describing an open position
within a company.
|FP Euroformac Página 16 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• Resume: A concise document summarizing an individual's education,
work experience, skills, and accomplishments.
• Interview: A formal discussion between a candidate and a potential
employer to assess suitability for a job.
• HR (Human Resources): The department responsible for managing
personnel, including recruitment and employee relations.
• Onboarding: The process of integrating a new employee into the
workplace and culture.
• Reference Check: The verification of a candidate's qualifications and
work history by contacting previous employers or references.
• Recruitment Agency: A company that helps organizations find
suitable candidates for job openings.
• Job Board: An online platform where employers can post job
openings, and job seekers can search for and apply for positions.
• Salary Negotiation: The process of discussing and agreeing on the
compensation package for a job.
• Candidate Experience: The overall experience a job applicant has
during the recruitment process.
• Job Fair: An event where employers and job seekers meet to discuss
job opportunities.
|FP Euroformac Página 17 de 22
< Inglés Técnico para Grado Superior> | Unidad 4
• Layoff: The temporary or permanent termination of employment due
to organizational changes, downsizing, or restructuring.
• Workforce Planning: Strategic planning to ensure that an
organization has the right talent to achieve its business goals.
• Retention: Efforts made by an organization to keep employees
engaged and prevent turnover.
• Job Description: A detailed outline of the duties, responsibilities, and
qualifications required for a specific job.
• Background Check: The process of investigating a candidate's
criminal, financial, and professional history.
• Contract-to-Hire: A temporary employment arrangement with the
possibility of a permanent position after a specified period.
• Employment Verification: Confirming the details of a candidate's
employment history and current employment status.
• Remote Work: Employment that allows employees to work from
locations other than the office, often facilitated by technology.
